pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–11; understand rainforests as BIODIVERSITY HOTSPOTS — ~6% of Earth's land surface holding over half of all known plant and animal species — and why that concentration makes them irreplaceable and a conservation priority.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS2 Geography (biomes, distribution of natural resources) and Science Y4 classification / Y6 living things; leads to KS3 Biology 'interdependence and biodiversity'.
• Standards — US: NGSS 3-LS4-3/-4 and MS-LS2-4/-5 (biodiversity, ecosystem services, and maintaining biodiversity).
• Operational details — the concept lives in a DISPROPORTION: a tiny slice of land, a giant slice of life. Teach it as a proportion contrast — 6% land vs >50% of known species — using a strong visual (two bars, or two pie slices). Ground it in a vivid concrete: a single hectare of Amazon can hold more tree species than all of Europe/North America combined. Be precise on caveats appropriate for the top tier: it's TROPICAL rainforests, and KNOWN/documented species (many are still undiscovered); credible figures range from 'more than half' up to WWF's '80% of documented species'. Land the 'so what': such concentration means clearing a small area destroys an outsized share of life → priority for protection.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (9): state ~6% land holds over half of all species. Tier B (10): explain why that concentration makes rainforests a conservation priority. Tier C (11): cite a concrete example (one hectare > all Europe's tree species) and add the 'tropical/known-species' caveat.
bestPractices: Teach the concept as a DISPROPORTION — tiny land share vs huge species share — with a direct side-by-side visual.
Ground the abstract percentage in a vivid concrete (one hectare holds more tree species than all of Europe).
State the caveats honestly at the top tier: tropical rainforests specifically, and KNOWN species (many undiscovered).
Land the 'so what': high concentration means clearing a small area destroys an outsized share of life → conservation priority.
Use up-to-date, authoritative figures (WWF, National Geographic) rather than advocacy aggregators.
keyRepresentations: Two proportion bars/pies: land ~6% vs known species >50%.
A one-hectare Amazon plot vs all-of-Europe tree-species comparison.
A gallery of example species (toucan, jaguar, dart frog) plus 'many still undiscovered'.
A 'shrink the sliver → lose a big chunk of species' cause-effect visual.
commonMisconceptions: 'Rainforests cover most of the Earth' — they cover only about 6% of land.
'Half the species means half of a small number' — it means over half of ALL known life on Earth.
'We know all the species already' — many, especially insects, remain undiscovered; figures are for KNOWN species.
'All rainforests (including temperate) hold this biodiversity' — the claim is specifically about tropical rainforests.
'Losing a small area is no big deal' — because life is so concentrated, small losses destroy an outsized share of species.

learn.summary: Learners (ages 9–11) build the concept that tropical rainforests are biodiversity hotspots: they cover only about 6% of Earth's land yet hold over half of all KNOWN plant and animal species. The central insight is a disproportion — a tiny slice of land, a giant slice of life — and its consequence: because so many species are packed into so little land, clearing tropical rainforest destroys habitat for far more species per area than most other land, and can permanently wipe out species found nowhere else, making protection a priority. Learners also distinguish biodiversity (variety of different species) from mere abundance (many animals of one kind).

activities.title: The mismatch made visible: 6% of land, over half of life
feedback: If a learner says rainforests must cover most of the Earth, point back to the thin sliver: tropical rainforests are only about 6% of land, yet still hold over half of known species.

If a learner reasons 'it's only 6%, so losing it isn't a big deal', have them re-run the shadow demo: contrast the 6% of land with the >50% of known species that live there and depend on that habitat.
If a learner thinks 'over half the species' means half of a small number, clarify it means over half of ALL known plant and animal life on Earth.
Reinforce that the example species shown are just a handful; captions note many more remain undiscovered, so the real variety is even greater.
activities.rationale: The concept lives in a proportion contrast, so a direct side-by-side visual of land share vs species share makes the disproportion concrete; grounding the abstract percentage in a vivid example (hundreds of tree species in a single hectare, sometimes compared to the tree variety of whole northern European regions) and a shadow demo showing how many species depend on the small sliver is intended to land the conservation consequence.
sourceClaims: Tropical forests cover just 6% of the planet's land surface but are some of the richest, most biodiverse places on Earth, home to a very large share of the world's species (WWF states 80% of documented species; other authorities state 'more than half of known species')
Rainforests cover roughly 2–6% of Earth's surface yet more than half of the world's known plant and animal species live in them; a single hectare can hold hundreds of tree species
learnerActions: Study a side-by-side pair of proportion bars (or two pie slices): one bar shows all of Earth's land with only a thin sliver (~6%, about a sixteenth) marked as tropical rainforest; the second bar shows all known living species with more than half marked as living in tropical rainforests.
Describe in your own words the mismatch you see between the land share and the species share.

Explore a drill-down (tap or reveal) that zooms the sliver to a single hectare of Amazon, with a caption presenting the often-cited illustration that it can hold more kinds of tree than all of northern Europe (authoritative sources confirm hundreds of tree species per hectare), and reveals example species — toucan, jaguar, poison dart frog — plus a note that many more species (especially insects) are still undiscovered.

Drag a shadow across the small green land sliver and watch the rainforest part of the species bar light up, showing how many known species depend on that small area; then explain why harming even part of it puts the homes of many species at risk (this is a model of concentration, not an exact count of species lost).
activities.intendedInsight: A tiny patch of the planet carries a staggering share of its known life; because life is so concentrated, clearing tropical rainforest destroys habitat for far more species per area than most other land, and can wipe out species found nowhere else — which is why protecting them matters so much.

activities.title: Estimate then reveal: predict the species share
feedback: If a learner guesses a small share, highlight the gap between their guess and the >50% reality, and tie it back to the 6%-of-land contrast.
Whatever the guess, confirm the two anchor figures explicitly: ~6% of land, over half of known species.
activities.rationale: An estimate-then-reveal interaction is intended to make the surprise active and can double as a check of understanding, while the core insight still rests on the proportion contrast that the cited figures support.
sourceClaims: Rainforests cover roughly 2–6% of Earth's surface yet more than half of the world's known plant and animal species live in them; a single hectare can hold hundreds of tree species
learnerActions: Before seeing the answer, predict what share of the world's known species live in tropical rainforests — for example by setting a slider or writing a percentage.
Reveal the actual figure (over half, i.e. >50%) shown against the fact that tropical rainforests are only about 6% of land, and compare it with your guess.
Say whether the real figure was higher or lower than you expected, and explain what surprised you.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners may underestimate how concentrated rainforest biodiversity is; committing to a prediction first is intended to make the true disproportion more memorable and surprising, though this prediction effect is a design hypothesis rather than a verified outcome.

activities.title: What 'biodiversity' really means, and why loss is irreversible
feedback: If a learner says biodiversity just means lots of animals, define it as the variety of different KINDS of species: 10,000 identical animals is low biodiversity, many different kinds is high.
If a learner says lost species exist elsewhere too, explain that many are endemic — found only in that forest — so losing the forest loses them entirely.

A full response links ~6% of land to >50% of known species, defines biodiversity as variety, and justifies the conservation priority; a partial response knows rainforests are rich but can't yet articulate the disproportion or the variety definition.
activities.rationale: The target concept pairs the disproportion with a correct definition of biodiversity as variety and the idea of endemism, so prompts that force learners to reason about both are intended to surface the common misconceptions directly; the disproportion element is supported by the cited WWF figures, while the biodiversity definition and endemism are inherited from the row's assessment rather than from a cited source.
sourceClaims: Tropical forests cover just 6% of the planet's land surface but are some of the richest, most biodiverse places on Earth, home to a very large share of the world's species (WWF states 80% of documented species; other authorities state 'more than half of known species')
learnerActions: Answer the diagnostic prompt: 'Rainforests cover only about 6% of Earth's land. If they're such a small slice of the planet, why do scientists say protecting them matters so much for life on Earth? Tell me why, and then tell me what biodiversity actually means here.'
Decide whether 10,000 animals that are all the same species would count as high biodiversity, and justify your answer.
Explain why we can't simply recreate a cleared rainforest's species somewhere else.
Write a short justification linking the 6%-of-land to the >50%-of-species figure and using it to argue for conservation priority.
activities.intendedInsight: Biodiversity means the VARIETY of different species, not just the number of animals; many tropical rainforest species are endemic (found nowhere else), so clearing their only habitat can wipe those species out entirely — this is why protection is a priority.

constraints: Be precise on caveats at the top tier: the claim is about TROPICAL rainforests specifically (not temperate rainforests), and about KNOWN/documented species — many, especially insects, remain undiscovered, so figures describe documented life.

Authoritative figures vary: credible sources range from 'more than half of known species' up to WWF's '80% of documented species'. Present a range rather than a single hard number, and cite authoritative sources (WWF, National Geographic) rather than advocacy aggregators.
Land-area figures also vary by source (National Geographic gives roughly 2–6%); use 'about 6%' as a teachable anchor while acknowledging the range.

A prediction slider or multiple-choice item can check that learners recall the two percentages and the conservation reasoning, but recognition/estimation alone does not show a learner can independently articulate the disproportion or define biodiversity — use an open written or spoken justification for that.

The shadow/shrink demo is a vivid representation of 'small area, outsized species loss'; keep it as an illustration of concentration, not a literal claim that species loss is exactly proportional to area cleared.

Tap-to-reveal species galleries and drill-downs are optional illustrative mechanisms; the core learning is the proportion contrast and its conservation consequence, which can also be shown with static paired bars or pie slices.

The 'one hectare holds more tree species than all of northern Europe' comparison is an original row claim not directly stated by the cited sources (National Geographic says only 'hundreds of tree species per hectare'); it is presented as a qualified illustration and the exact comparison and wording should be verified against an authoritative source before publishing.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source row marks the National Geographic and DfE claims as verified:false and the WWF claim as verified:true; the two biodiversity percentage figures (>50% vs WWF's 80%) and the land-area figures (~6% vs 2–6%) come from different authorities and are not identical, so the activities present ranges rather than asserting one exact number.

The estimate-then-reveal 'prediction makes it more memorable' rationale and the 'learners underestimate' claim are design hypotheses; no cited source establishes this effect, so they are stated with proposed/intended wording. The claim attached to Activity 2 supports only the revealed proportion content, not the prediction mechanism.

The legacy row rated 3D and conversation formats as 'poor' with claims like '3D adds nothing' and 'no essential persona'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have not been carried forward as universal claims. A proportion-contrast visual is a good fit here, but this does not prove other media cannot teach the concept.

The 'one hectare holds more tree species than all of Europe/northern Europe' example appears with slightly different wording across the row (Europe, Europe/North America combined, northern Europe) and National Geographic's claim says only 'hundreds of tree species per hectare'; the comparison is retained as a qualified vivid illustration but exact phrasing should be checked against the cited source before publishing.

Endemism and the biodiversity-as-variety definition are inherited from the row's assessment content and are not directly backed by a cited source; treat as topic-standard framing pending source confirmation.

probeDeeper: Rainforests are 6% of land but hold over half of known species — what does that comparison tell you?
What does the word 'biodiversity' mean in your own words?
Why can't we just recreate a rainforest's species somewhere else if it's cleared?
Would 10,000 animals that are all the same species count as high biodiversity? Why or why not?
assess.correctAnswer: Because that tiny 6% of land holds more than half of all the world's known plant and animal species — an astonishing concentration of DIFFERENT kinds of life (a single hectare can hold more tree species than all of northern Europe). Biodiversity means the VARIETY of different species, not just the number of animals. Losing that small area would wipe out a huge share of the planet's species, many found nowhere else — which is why it's a top conservation priority.

errorPatterns.pattern: small area means it matters little — 'it's only 6%, so losing it isn't a big deal'
errorPatterns.nextMove: contrast the 6% of land with >50% of species; a tiny area holds most of Earth's variety of life
errorPatterns.distractor: It's only a small part of the Earth, so it doesn't matter much
errorPatterns.revealedBy: reasons from land area alone that rainforests are minor

errorPatterns.pattern: biodiversity just means lots of animals — misses VARIETY of different species
errorPatterns.nextMove: define biodiversity as the variety of different species; many kinds, many found nowhere else
errorPatterns.revealedBy: equates biodiversity with large numbers rather than many kinds

errorPatterns.pattern: species lost here exist elsewhere too — 'we can find them in other forests'
errorPatterns.nextMove: many are endemic (found only there); losing the forest loses them entirely
errorPatterns.revealedBy: assumes rainforest species are common worldwide

responseLevels.gap: Thinks a small area means low importance, or biodiversity = many animals.
responseLevels.full: Explains that ~6% of land holds >50% of known species (a concentration of variety, much of it endemic), defines biodiversity as the variety of different species, and justifies the conservation priority.
responseLevels.partial: Knows rainforests are very rich in life but can't articulate the 6%-vs->50% disproportion or define biodiversity as variety.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Rainforests cover only about 6% of Earth's land. If they're such a small slice of the planet, why do scientists say protecting them matters so much for life on Earth? Tell me why, and then tell me what 'biodiversity' actually means here.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reasons 'small area means unimportant' or 'biodiversity means lots of animals' misses the concentration-of-variety point; the concept child links 6%-of-land to >50%-of-species and defines biodiversity as variety. The reason-tier forces the disproportion-plus-variety reasoning.
